title: The Rise of Science
orientation: Russell argues that the modern world, in mental outlook, begins not with the Italian Renaissance or the Reformation but with seventeenth-century science, and traces its creation through four pre-eminent figures -- Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, and Newton. The chapter is less a chapter of philosophy in the narrow sense than an account of the scientific achievement that made modern philosophy (beginning with Descartes) possible, and it closes by drawing out the philosophical and cultural consequences of the new science: the removal of animism and purpose from physics, the diminishment and then paradoxical inflation of human self-importance, and the shift of physical law from describing shapes of orbits to describing accelerations.
historical_background: Russell dates the true mental transition to modernity to the seventeenth century: 'No Italian of the Renaissance would have been unintelligible to Plato or Aristotle; Luther would have horrified Thomas Aquinas, but would not have been difficult for him to understand. With the seventeenth century it is different.' Copernicus (1473-1543), a Polish ecclesiastic of 'unimpeachable orthodoxy,' delayed publishing his heliocentric theory from fear of ecclesiastical censure; his book, dedicated to the Pope, escaped official Catholic condemnation until Galileo's era, since the Church before the Council of Trent and the revived Inquisition was more liberal. Tycho Brahe's exhaustive astronomical observations then supplied Kepler with the data to refine the heliocentric model, and Galileo's dynamics and telescope, followed by Newton's synthesis, completed the transformation.
philosophical_problems: Is celestial and terrestrial motion governed by the same laws, or fundamentally different ones (as Aristotle held)?
Should scientific hypotheses be accepted only when proven, or tentatively, as working, revisable guesses -- and what distinguishes the scientific attitude from dogmatism?
Does removing 'force,' purpose, and animism from physics eliminate the need for a Creator or active God in explaining nature?
Is motion (and rotation) absolute or purely relative, and what follows philosophically either way?
What is man's place in a universe whose scale and mechanism no longer center on the earth or evidently serve human purposes?

philosophers_discussed.name: Nicolaus Copernicus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Credited with the heliocentric hypothesis (sun-centered universe, with the earth's diurnal rotation and annual revolution), presented cautiously as a hypothesis to avoid ecclesiastical censure. Russell stresses his work was still 'Pythagorean' in spirit (circular, uniform motions, aesthetic bias, retained epicycles) rather than fully modern, but praises his combination of patient knowledge of existing data with the boldness to prefer a more 'economical hypothesis.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Tycho Brahe
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Discussed as an important observer rather than theorist, who proposed an intermediate geo-heliocentric system but whose real importance was his patient, decades-long accumulation of precise planetary and stellar observations (including evidence against Aristotle's doctrine of an unchanging heavens, from a new star in 1572 and from comets), later used by his assistant Kepler.

philosophers_discussed.name: Johannes Kepler
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Discussed as 'one of the most notable examples of what can be achieved by patience without much in the way of genius,' whose three laws of planetary motion (elliptical orbits, equal areas in equal times, and the relation between orbital period and distance) gave the heliocentric theory its 'full simplicity,' discarding the ancient aesthetic prejudice in favor of circular motion despite being partly motivated by his own Pythagorean, quasi-mystical inclinations.

philosophers_discussed.name: Galileo Galilei
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Presented as 'the greatest of the founders of modern science, with the possible exception of Newton,' credited with discovering the importance of acceleration and the law of inertia, the law of falling bodies, the parabolic path of projectiles and the parallelogram law of forces, and with using the telescope to discover the phases of Venus and the moons of Jupiter, which he defended against traditionalist ridicule; his 1616 and 1633 condemnations by the Inquisition are recounted as ending Italian science for centuries while failing to stop the heliocentric theory's spread.

philosophers_discussed.name: Isaac Newton
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Presented as achieving 'the final and complete triumph' anticipated by his three predecessors, deriving Kepler's laws from his own laws of motion and the inverse-square law of universal gravitation, and thereby unifying terrestrial and celestial mechanics; Russell notes the danger that Newton's authority, like Aristotle's before him, threatened to become 'an insuperable barrier to progress' for a century after his death.

philosophers_discussed.name: Martin Luther
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Quoted denouncing Copernicus as 'an upstart astrologer' who contradicts Scripture (the story of Joshua commanding the sun to stand still), illustrating that Protestant clergy were, per Russell, 'at least as bigoted as Catholic ecclesiastics' toward the new astronomy.

philosophers_discussed.name: John Calvin
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Quoted rejecting Copernicus by citing Psalm XCIII ('The world also is stablished, that it cannot be moved') and asking who would place Copernicus's authority above the Holy Spirit's.

schools_discussed: Pythagoreanism (as a residual influence on Copernicus and Kepler)
Aristotelian natural philosophy (as the view science overturns)

core_concepts.name: The law of inertia and the abandonment of 'natural' places and motions
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Before Galileo, people thought heavenly bodies naturally moved in circles and earthly objects naturally moved in straight lines but would gradually stop unless kept moving. Galileo showed instead that any moving body, left alone, keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed forever; any change in speed or direction needs a 'force' to explain it. This is the same principle on earth and in the heavens.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Galileo's principle, later codified by Newton as the first law of motion: 'every body, if let alone, will continue to move in a straight line with uniform velocity; any change, either in the rapidity or the direction of motion, requires to be explained as due to the action of some "force."' Acceleration -- change of velocity in magnitude or direction -- becomes the central concept of dynamics, replacing Aristotle's distinction between 'natural' circular celestial motion and 'natural' rectilinear terrestrial motion that ceases without continued impulse.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It unified terrestrial and celestial physics under one law, explained puzzles the Copernican system could not (such as why a dropped stone falls at the foot of a tower rather than to its west, despite the earth's rotation), and became the foundation of Newton's synthesis.
core_concepts.historical_origin: First established by Galileo; enunciated formally by Newton as the first law of motion.
examples: A dropped stone retains the rotational velocity of the tower it falls from, so it lands at the tower's foot, not to the west
The law of falling bodies: acceleration is constant (about 32 feet per second per second) and the same for heavy and light bodies alike
competing_positions: Aristotle's view that circular motion is 'natural' to heavenly bodies and rectilinear motion 'natural' but self-exhausting for terrestrial bodies
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly incorporated by Newton as the first law of motion, and foundational to Descartes's mechanistic physics (Chapter IX), which likewise assumes uniform rectilinear motion absent external impact.

core_concepts.name: Kepler's three laws of planetary motion
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Kepler discovered that planets do not move in perfect circles (as every astronomer before him had assumed) but in ellipses with the sun at one focus; that a planet speeds up when near the sun and slows down when far from it, sweeping out equal areas in equal times; and that there is a precise mathematical relationship between a planet's orbital period and its average distance from the sun.
core_concepts.precise_definition: First law: the planets describe elliptic orbits, of which the sun occupies one focus. Second law: the line joining a planet to the sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Third law: the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its average distance from the sun.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: The first law required abandoning the millennia-old aesthetic assumption that celestial motion must be circular (since circles were considered the 'perfect' figure proper to divine or semi-divine heavenly bodies); the third law later provided, as Russell notes, 'the proof (as far as the solar system is concerned) of Newton's law of the inverse square for gravitation.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: The first two laws published in 1609, the third in 1619, based substantially on Tycho Brahe's observational data, especially of Mars.
examples: The precise fit of elliptical orbits to Tycho Brahe's recorded positions of Mars, where circular models (including Copernicus's) failed
competing_positions: Ptolemaic and Copernican systems relying on circles and epicycles
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly used by Newton to derive the inverse-square law of gravitation.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Kepler's Pythagorean, sun-worshipping inclinations (despite being 'a good Protestant') illustrate the mixture of mystical and rigorously empirical motives in early modern science.

core_concepts.name: Newton's law of universal gravitation and the unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Newton showed that the same force that makes an apple fall to earth also keeps the moon orbiting the earth and the planets orbiting the sun: every body attracts every other body with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. From this single formula he could deduce planetary orbits, satellite motion, cometary paths, and the tides.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Newton's law: 'Every body attracts every other with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them,' derived by showing that Kepler's three laws are equivalent to the claim that every planet has, at every moment, an acceleration toward the sun that varies inversely as the square of the distance.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It completed the 'final and complete triumph' of the new astronomy and dynamics, and its success was so total that, Russell notes, 'Newton was in danger of becoming another Aristotle,' with English science not freeing itself from his authority for a century.
examples: Deduction of the motions of planets and satellites, cometary orbits (including Halley's calculations), and the tides
Later confirmation that minute departures of planetary orbits from perfect ellipses were also deducible from the law
objections: Later physics found the concept of 'force' itself superfluous: 'to say that this is due to the "force" of gravitation is merely verbal, like saying that opium makes people sleep because it has a dormitive virtue'
competing_positions: Descartes's vortex theory of planetary motion (mentioned in Chapter IX), which Newton's theory gradually displaced, first in England and later in France
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Discussed by Russell as eventually modified, but not overturned in its basic form (laws stated in terms of accelerations), by Einstein.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Provoked the theological reflection that God might have set the planets moving but need not intervene further -- discussed under the concept of the removal of animism.

core_concepts.name: The removal of animism and purpose from physics
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Ancient and medieval thinkers assumed that only living things move themselves, and that the heavens must be kept moving by souls or spirits (or, in Aristotle, by divine 'unmoved movers'). Once the law of inertia showed that lifeless matter, once set moving, keeps moving forever without continued animating cause, there was no longer any scientific need for souls, spirits, or ongoing divine intervention to explain the physical universe's motion.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's account: 'Lifeless matter, once set moving, will continue to move for ever unless stopped by some external cause... The solar system... was kept going by its own momentum and its own laws; no outside interference was needed.' God might still be needed to set the mechanism working initially, but 'when He had done this... everything went on by itself without further need of divine intervention,' and even the necessity of an initial Creator became doubtful once Laplace suggested the planets might have formed naturally from the sun.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It represents the single largest philosophical consequence of the scientific revolution for the concept of God and of natural explanation, and Russell notes it was 'disturbing to orthodoxy,' even though most scientists of the era remained personally pious.
core_concepts.historical_origin: A direct consequence of Galileo's and Newton's laws of motion, later extended by Laplace's nebular hypothesis.
examples: Aristotle's forty-seven or fifty-five 'unmoved movers,' the ancient Greek habit of regarding the sun and planets as gods or moved by gods
Laplace's suggestion that the planets grew naturally out of the sun, pushing back the need for a Creator further still
competing_positions: Aristotle's animistic cosmology, in which soul must continuously act on matter to sustain motion
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Anticipates the mechanistic worldview fully developed by Descartes (Chapter IX), who treats animal bodies as automata governed entirely by physical law.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly concerns the diminishing scientific need to invoke God's continuous action, a central tension for seventeenth-century natural theology.

core_concepts.name: The transformation of man's place in the universe
core_concepts.plain_explanation: In the medieval picture, the earth sat at the center of a cosmos designed around human concerns. Once Copernicus, Kepler, and Newton showed the earth to be a minor planet of an unremarkable star in an immense mechanical universe, it became hard to believe the whole apparatus existed for the sake of small creatures on a 'pin-point' -- yet, paradoxically, the very triumphs of science that should have humbled humanity instead revived human pride and self-satisfaction.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's account of the double effect: the Copernican and Newtonian universe 'should have been humbling to human pride, but in fact the contrary effect was produced, for the triumphs of science revived human pride,' displacing the earlier medieval 'sense of sin' with confidence exemplified by Pope's couplet, 'Nature and Nature's laws lay hid in night. / God said "Let Newton be," and all was light.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It illustrates a recurring irony in intellectual history that Russell highlights: a discovery that logically diminishes human cosmic importance can psychologically and culturally increase human self-confidence, especially when combined with contemporaneous European commercial and imperial expansion.
core_concepts.historical_origin: A cumulative cultural effect of the astronomical and physical discoveries recounted through the chapter, reaching its clearest expression by the later seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries.
examples: European material and imperial self-satisfaction (conquest of the Americas, influence in Africa, India, China, Japan) as a parallel, non-scientific source of the same growing self-confidence
competing_positions: The medieval theological outlook, in which humility before God was 'both right and prudent, for God would punish pride'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly concerns the theological doctrine of sin and damnation, which Russell suggests became harder to sustain in full medieval severity once human intellectual achievement seemed so impressive.

core_concepts.name: The relativity of motion and the abandonment of absolute space and time
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Newton believed space and time existed independently of the objects and events in them, and thought absolute rotation (as opposed to relative motion) could be empirically detected, for example by the way water climbs the sides of a rotating bucket. Later physics increasingly treated all motion, including rotation, as purely relative, and merged space and time into a single space-time -- a change Russell flags as one of the most important since Newton, though one he declines to pursue in depth in this book.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell notes the empirical puzzle: 'If all motion is relative, the difference between the hypothesis that the earth rotates and the hypothesis that the heavens revolve is purely verbal... But if the heavens revolve, the stars move faster than light, which is considered impossible' -- a difficulty he says is not fully resolved but is 'sufficiently satisfying to cause almost all physicists to accept the view that motion and space are purely relative.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It marks a genuine change from the Newtonian picture that would matter greatly for twentieth-century philosophy of physics, even though Russell treats it here only briefly as a signpost toward material he sets aside for this book.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Traced back to Newton's own bucket-of-water argument for absolute rotation, later challenged and revised by relativity theory and the amalgamation of space and time into space-time.
examples: Foucault's pendulum, taken as a demonstration of the earth's rotation
competing_positions: Newton's own belief in absolute space and time, independent of bodies and events
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Connects back to the earlier discussion of Democritus's views on space (noted explicitly by Russell) and forward to unnamed but implied twentieth-century relativity physics.

arguments.title: Why the scientific attitude, not the specific content of early theories, is what distinguished the new science
premises: E. A. Burtt's The Metaphysical Foundations of Modern Physical Science shows that in Copernicus's time there were no known facts compelling adoption of his system, and several facts that militated against it, and that 'contemporary empiricists... would have been the first to scoff out of court the new philosophy of the universe.'
Burtt uses this to suggest modern science's discoveries were, in effect, lucky accidents springing from assumptions as unwarranted as medieval superstitions.

But what distinguishes the man of science is not the specific content of his beliefs but how and why he holds them: tentatively, based on evidence, revisable -- not dogmatically, based on authority or intuition.
arguments.conclusion: Copernicus was right to call his own theory a hypothesis, and his opponents were wrong to consider new hypotheses undesirable; the scientific attitude, not the correctness of any particular early guess, is the real achievement of this period.
arguments.explanation: Russell uses this argument to defend the founders of modern science against Burtt's suggestion that their success was mere epistemic luck, relocating the significance of the Scientific Revolution in method (patient observation plus bold, revisable hypothesis) rather than in any single theory being immediately provable.
objections: Burtt's implicit objection that the founders' discoveries rested on many unwarranted metaphysical assumptions of their own
implications: Frames the chapter's recurring praise of 'immense patience in observation, and great boldness in framing hypotheses' as the joint, historically rare combination that defines genuine scientific achievement (found together, Russell argues, in Copernicus and his successors but in no ancient or medieval thinker).

arguments.title: From Kepler's three laws to Newton's law of universal gravitation
premises: Kepler's three laws describe planetary orbits (ellipses, equal areas in equal times, and the period-distance relation) purely geometrically and empirically, without explaining their cause.

Newton showed that Kepler's three laws are together equivalent to the proposition that every planet, at every moment, has an acceleration toward the sun varying inversely as the square of the distance.
The same inverse-square relation, applied to the earth and moon, and to falling bodies on earth's surface, explains the moon's motion and terrestrial gravity by the same formula.
Newton defined 'force' as the cause of change of motion (acceleration).
arguments.conclusion: Every body in the universe attracts every other body with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them -- the law of universal gravitation, from which the motions of planets, satellites, comets, and tides can all be deduced.
arguments.explanation: This argument is the chapter's central scientific achievement: it shows Newton did not merely add a fourth law alongside Kepler's three but derived a single, more fundamental principle from which Kepler's empirical laws (and terrestrial mechanics) follow as special cases, unifying what had been treated as separate domains (celestial and terrestrial motion) since Aristotle.
objections: Later physics found the concept of 'force' explanatorily superfluous, since all that is truly observed is the relation between acceleration and configuration
implications: Establishes the pattern, followed throughout later physics, of unifying apparently distinct phenomena under a single mathematical law.

key_distinctions: Circular, 'perfect' celestial motion (ancient and Copernican assumption) vs. elliptical orbits (Kepler's first law)

'Natural' motion as self-sustaining vs. self-exhausting, depending on whether a body is celestial or terrestrial (Aristotle) vs. uniform rectilinear motion as universally 'natural' absent external force (Galileo's law of inertia)
Dogmatic acceptance of authority vs. the tentative, evidence-based, revisable scientific attitude Russell credits to Copernicus and his successors
Absolute space and time, independent of bodies and events (Newton) vs. the later view that motion and space are purely relative

'Force' as an imaginatively felt cause of motion (Newton's own conception) vs. 'force' as a superfluous verbal label for observed relations between acceleration and configuration (the modern physicist's view, per Russell)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell explicitly contrasts the new science with Aristotle (whose doctrine that change is confined to the sublunary sphere, and whose 'unmoved movers,' both proved obstacles to progress) and Plato and Aquinas (neither of whom, Russell says, could have understood Newton, unlike the mutual intelligibility of Renaissance Italians with Plato and Aristotle, or of Luther with Aquinas). He also references Democritus's earlier views on absolute space and Aristarchus of Samos as an ancient anticipator (unknown to Copernicus) of heliocentrism and, uniquely among the ancients besides Copernicus's own tradition, a combiner of patient observation with bold hypothesis.
connections_to_later_philosophers: The chapter is explicitly presented as necessary background for understanding Descartes, 'who was in a sense the founder of modern philosophy' and 'was himself one of the creators of seventeenth-century science'; it also anticipates the mechanistic, deterministic worldview central to Hobbes (Chapter VIII) and Descartes (Chapter IX), and its account of Newtonian 'force' being later found superfluous anticipates general Enlightenment and post-Enlightenment developments in physics that Russell notes but sets aside (quantum mechanics, relativity, space-time).
political_social_context: Russell connects the scientific revolution to broader currents of European self-confidence and expansion: the growing wealth of Western Europe, its colonization of the Americas, and its influence in Africa, India, China, and Japan are cited as parallel, non-scientific sources of the era's growing human self-satisfaction, alongside the intellectual triumphs of Newtonian science.
religion_science_culture_context: The chapter is saturated with religion-science conflict and negotiation: Copernicus's caution and orthodoxy; Luther's and Calvin's scriptural objections to heliocentrism; Galileo's condemnation by the Inquisition in 1616 and 1633; the seven-heavenly-bodies controversy over Jupiter's moons (tied to the supposed sacredness of the number seven); and the broader theological unease at the removal of animism, purpose, and continuous divine intervention from physical explanation, even though, Russell stresses, most of the scientists themselves remained personally devout.
russell_presentation: Russell presents the rise of science as the true dividing line of modernity, crediting Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, and Newton (in ascending order of achievement, with Galileo and Newton as the two greatest) with combining, for the first time together in a sustained way, patient empirical observation and bold, revisable hypothesis-making. He defends the scientific attitude explicitly against E. A. Burtt's charge that early modern science's success was merely lucky, arguing that what matters is method (tentative, evidence-based belief) rather than the immediate provability of any particular early theory. He is admiring but not uncritical: he notes Copernicus's residual Pythagorean aesthetic bias, Kepler's quasi-mystical motivations, and the danger that Newton's overwhelming authority threatened, like Aristotle's before him, to freeze rather than advance further inquiry. He closes the chapter by drawing out the era's deepest philosophical consequences -- the removal of animism and purpose from physical explanation, the destabilizing effect on orthodox theology, and the paradoxical way in which a cosmologically humbling discovery (earth's insignificance) produced not humility but a new, scientifically-fueled human self-confidence.
critical_context: Russell explicitly engages with a serious scholarly challenge to his own admiring account -- E. A. Burtt's The Metaphysical Foundations of Modern Physical Science (1925), which argued that the founders of modern science relied on many unwarrantable metaphysical assumptions and that their success was closer to a lucky accident than a triumph of superior method; Russell rejects Burtt's deflationary reading but preserves it in the text as a genuine, named counter-position rather than dismissing it silently. Later historians of science have further nuanced Russell's confident narrative of steady 'progress,' noting, for example, greater continuity between medieval natural philosophy and early modern science than this chapter's sharp seventeenth-century dividing line suggests -- a point in the same spirit as, though not identical to, Burtt's own critique.
key_takeaways: Russell identifies the seventeenth century, not the Italian Renaissance or the Reformation, as the true beginning of the modern mental outlook, because of the transformative achievement of Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, and Newton.

Galileo's law of inertia (and Newton's codification of it as the first law of motion) unified terrestrial and celestial dynamics under a single principle: uniform motion is 'natural' unless changed by an external force.

Kepler's three laws (elliptical orbits, equal areas in equal times, and the period-distance relation) required abandoning the ancient aesthetic assumption that celestial motion must be circular, and later supplied evidence for Newton's law of gravitation.

Newton's law of universal gravitation unified celestial and terrestrial mechanics under one inverse-square formula, completing 'the final and complete triumph' of the scientific revolution, though his overwhelming authority also risked becoming a new barrier to progress.

The new science removed animism and purpose from physical explanation, reducing (though not eliminating) the scientific need to invoke continuous divine action, which Russell says genuinely unsettled orthodox theology.

Paradoxically, a cosmology that should have humbled humanity (a minor planet of an undistinguished star) instead fed a new, scientifically-grounded human pride, reinforced by simultaneous European commercial and imperial expansion.
study_notes:
This chapter is best read as connective tissue: Russell tells you directly that it exists to prepare readers to understand Descartes, 'who was in a sense the founder of modern philosophy' but was also 'one of the creators of seventeenth-century science.' As you work through the astronomy and dynamics, keep two separate threads distinct: (1) the specific content of the science (heliocentrism, elliptical orbits, inertia, universal gravitation) and (2) Russell's claim about scientific method itself -- that what makes this period historically decisive is not that any particular early hypothesis was immediately provable, but that its proponents combined patient, evidence-based observation with a willingness to revise bold hypotheses, as opposed to defending inherited authority. His engagement with Burtt's skeptical counter-argument is a good model of how to take a serious objection seriously rather than dismiss it.

The chapter's second half, from Galileo onward, deliberately widens from astronomy and dynamics to instruments (microscope, telescope, thermometer, barometer, air pump), to other sciences (magnetism, circulation of the blood, microscopy, chemistry), and to pure mathematics (logarithms, coordinate geometry, calculus) -- a reminder that the 'rise of science' Russell describes was a broad, coordinated advance, not the work of astronomy alone. Its final movement, from 'the removal of animism' through 'man's place in the universe' to the abandonment of absolute space and time, is where the chapter earns its place in a philosophy history rather than a pure history of science: each of these consequences reappears, transformed, in the metaphysics of Descartes, Hobbes, and later rationalists and empiricists covered in the rest of Book III.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that the sun, not the earth, is at the center of the solar system, with the earth both spinning on its axis and orbiting the sun.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The astronomical model, proposed cautiously by Copernicus and confirmed and refined by Kepler, Galileo, and Newton, in which the sun occupies (approximately) the center of the planetary system and the earth undergoes both diurnal rotation and annual revolution, displacing the geocentric Ptolemaic model.
related_concepts: Kepler's three laws of planetary motion

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The principle that a moving object keeps moving in a straight line at a constant speed forever unless something acts on it to change its speed or direction.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Galileo's discovery, formalized by Newton as the first law of motion, that uniform rectilinear motion, not rest or circular motion, is the 'natural' state of a body absent external force; acceleration (change of velocity in magnitude or direction) thereby becomes the central explanatory concept of dynamics.
related_concepts: The law of inertia and the abandonment of 'natural' places and motions

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Any change in an object's speed or direction of motion -- not just speeding up, but also slowing down or turning.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Change of velocity, whether in magnitude or direction; Galileo's key discovery in dynamics, later the quantity that Newton's laws of motion and gravitation are formulated to explain, and which Russell notes remains the basis of dynamical law even after the concept of 'force' was found dispensable.
related_concepts: The law of inertia and the abandonment of 'natural' places and motions
Newton's law of universal gravitation and the unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Newton's law that every object in the universe pulls on every other object, with a strength that depends on how massive they are and how far apart they are.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Newton's law that every body attracts every other body with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, derived from showing that Kepler's three laws are equivalent to a specific inverse-square acceleration toward the sun.
related_concepts: Newton's law of universal gravitation and the unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics

questions.prompt: Why does Russell locate the true beginning of the 'modern world,' in mental outlook, in the seventeenth century rather than the Italian Renaissance or the Reformation?
questions.answer: Because Renaissance Italians would have been intelligible to Plato or Aristotle, and Luther, though he would have horrified Aquinas, would not have been difficult for him to understand -- but Plato, Aristotle, Aquinas, and Occam 'could not have made head or tail of Newton,' marking a genuine break introduced by seventeenth-century science.
questions.explanation: This is Russell's opening thesis for the chapter, explaining why he devotes an entire chapter of a philosophy history to scientific rather than strictly philosophical figures.

questions.prompt: Which astronomer's decades of patient, precise observations -- including evidence from a 1572 new star and from comets against Aristotle's doctrine of an unchanging heaven -- directly supplied the data Kepler needed to discover his laws?
questions.explanation: Brahe was important 'not as a theorist, but as an observer'; Kepler became his assistant late in Brahe's life.

questions.prompt: State Kepler's three laws of planetary motion in your own words.
questions.answer: First: planets move in ellipses with the sun at one focus. Second: the line from planet to sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times (so planets move faster near the sun, slower far from it). Third: the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its average distance from the sun.
questions.explanation: The first two laws were published in 1609, the third in 1619; the third later helped confirm Newton's inverse-square law.

questions.prompt: How did Galileo's law of inertia resolve a long-standing objection to the Copernican theory concerning falling bodies?
questions.answer: Critics argued that if the earth rotates, a stone dropped from a tower should land west of the tower's foot because the earth would have slipped away beneath it during the fall. Galileo's law of inertia explained that the stone retains the rotational velocity it shared with the tower before being dropped, so (apart from a negligible eastward effect from the tower's greater height and speed) it lands at the foot of the tower as observed.
questions.explanation: This shows how a new dynamical principle could resolve an empirical puzzle that had genuinely stumped defenders of Copernicus.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct how Newton derived his law of universal gravitation from Kepler's three laws.
questions.answer: Newton showed that Kepler's three laws together are equivalent to the claim that every planet, at every moment, has an acceleration toward the sun varying inversely as the square of its distance from the sun. He then showed the same inverse-square relation, applied to the earth, explains both the moon's motion and the acceleration of falling bodies on earth's surface. Defining force as the cause of change of motion, he concluded that every body attracts every other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
questions.explanation: This derivation is what let Newton deduce planetary and satellite motions, cometary orbits, and the tides from a single law.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, what did the discovery that lifeless matter, once moving, keeps moving without continued animating cause imply for the theological picture of the universe?
questions.answer: It removed the scientific need for continuous divine (or animistic) intervention to sustain the motion of the heavens; God might still be needed to set the mechanism going initially and decree the law of gravitation, but afterward 'everything went on by itself' -- and even the need for an initial Creator became doubtful once Laplace suggested the planets might have formed naturally from the sun.
questions.explanation: Russell treats this as one of the era's most significant, if unintended, philosophical and theological consequences.

questions.prompt: Compare the reactions of Luther and Calvin to Copernicus's heliocentric theory with the eventual reception of the theory among scientists.
questions.answer: Luther called Copernicus 'an upstart astrologer' who contradicted Scripture's account of Joshua commanding the sun (not the earth) to stand still; Calvin cited Psalm XCIII to argue the world 'cannot be moved' and asked who would place Copernicus's authority above the Holy Spirit's. Despite this bigotry, which Russell says matched that of Catholic ecclesiastics, heliocentrism was eventually confirmed and extended by Kepler, Galileo, and Newton, and Protestant countries (having weaker clerical power, per Chapter V) ultimately allowed more liberty of scientific speculation than Catholic ones.
questions.explanation: This links the chapter back to Chapter V's argument about the structurally weaker power of Protestant clergy.

flashcards.front: What four men does Russell name as pre-eminent in the creation of modern science?
In what year was Copernicus's chief work, De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium, published?
What astronomer's decades of precise observation supplied the data behind Kepler's laws?
State Kepler's first law of planetary motion.
flashcards.back: The planets describe elliptic orbits, of which the sun occupies one focus.

flashcards.front: State Kepler's second law of planetary motion.
flashcards.back: The line joining a planet to the sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times.

flashcards.front: State Kepler's third law of planetary motion.
flashcards.back: The square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its average distance from the sun.

flashcards.front: What did Galileo discover about the acceleration of falling bodies?
flashcards.back: It is constant and the same for all bodies, heavy or light, apart from air resistance.

flashcards.front: What is the law of inertia?
flashcards.back: A body left alone continues to move in a straight line at constant velocity forever; any change in speed or direction requires a 'force.'

flashcards.front: What did Galileo discover with his telescope regarding Jupiter?
flashcards.back: Jupiter's four satellites ('sidera medicea'), which obey Kepler's laws.

flashcards.front: In what years was Galileo condemned by the Inquisition, and what did he do in 1633?
flashcards.back: First privately in 1616, then publicly in 1633, when he recanted and promised never again to maintain the earth rotates or revolves.

flashcards.front: State Newton's law of universal gravitation.
flashcards.back: Every body attracts every other body with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

flashcards.front: In what year was Newton's Principia published?
How did Luther and Calvin each respond to Copernicus's theory?
flashcards.back: Luther called him 'an upstart astrologer' contradicting Scripture; Calvin cited Psalm XCIII and asked who would place Copernicus's authority above the Holy Spirit's.

flashcards.front: What philosophical change did the law of inertia bring about regarding the need for souls or spirits to explain motion?
flashcards.back: It removed the need for animating souls/spirits to sustain motion, since lifeless matter, once moving, keeps moving on its own.

flashcards.front: What book does Russell cite as challenging the idea that early modern science's success was due to superior method rather than luck?
flashcards.back: E. A. Burtt's The Metaphysical Foundations of Modern Physical Science (1925).

quiz.prompt: Which four scientists does Russell name as pre-eminent in the creation of modern science?
quiz.explanation: Russell writes: 'Four great men -- Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, and Newton -- are pre-eminent in the creation of science.'
quiz.related_concept: Kepler's three laws of planetary motion

quiz.prompt: According to Kepler's first law, what shape do planetary orbits take?
options: Ellipses with the sun at one focus
quiz.explanation: Kepler's first law states planets describe elliptic orbits with the sun at one focus, overturning the ancient assumption of circular motion.
quiz.related_concept: Kepler's three laws of planetary motion

quiz.prompt: Galileo's law of inertia holds that a moving body will gradually slow down and stop unless continually pushed.
quiz.explanation: The opposite is true: a body left alone continues moving in a straight line at constant velocity forever, unless acted on by an external force.
quiz.related_concept: The law of inertia and the abandonment of 'natural' places and motions

quiz.prompt: What did Newton show about the relationship between Kepler's three laws and gravitation?
options: That Kepler's laws were entirely wrong and had to be replaced
That Kepler's three laws are equivalent to every planet having an acceleration toward the sun varying inversely as the square of the distance
That Kepler's laws applied only to Mars
That Kepler's laws contradicted the law of inertia
quiz.explanation: Newton proved Kepler's three laws equivalent to an inverse-square acceleration toward the sun, from which he derived universal gravitation.
quiz.related_concept: Newton's law of universal gravitation and the unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics

quiz.prompt: Why, according to Russell, did the law of inertia have significant theological implications?
options: It proved the existence of God directly
It removed the scientific need for souls or continuous divine intervention to sustain the motion of matter
It confirmed Aristotle's doctrine of unmoved movers
It showed that comets were divine omens
quiz.explanation: Once lifeless matter, once set moving, continues to move by itself, there is no longer a scientific need for animating spirits or continuous divine action.
quiz.related_concept: The removal of animism and purpose from physics

quiz.prompt: Newton's law of gravitation states that force is proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the ____ of the distance between them.
quiz.explanation: This is the inverse-square law of universal gravitation.
quiz.related_concept: Newton's law of universal gravitation and the unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics

quiz.prompt: What argument does E. A. Burtt make about the founders of modern science, according to Russell, and how does Russell respond?
options: Burtt argues their success was inevitable given the evidence; Russell agrees fully

Burtt argues their discoveries were closer to lucky accidents resting on unwarranted assumptions; Russell responds that what matters is their tentative, evidence-based method, not the immediate provability of their theories
Burtt argues Copernicus plagiarized Aristarchus; Russell disputes this on textual grounds
Burtt argues Newton's physics was refuted by Kepler; Russell finds this persuasive
quiz.explanation: Russell explicitly rejects Burtt's deflationary reading, relocating the achievement in scientific method rather than immediate proof.
quiz.related_concept: Why the scientific attitude, not the specific content of early theories, is what distinguished the new science

quiz.prompt: Russell suggests that the Copernican revolution, by making the earth cosmically insignificant, in fact produced greater human pride rather than humility.
quiz.explanation: Russell says this 'should have been humbling to human pride, but in fact the contrary effect was produced, for the triumphs of science revived human pride.'
quiz.related_concept: The transformation of man's place in the universe

quiz.prompt: According to the chapter's closing discussion, why did later physics abandon the concept of 'force' even while keeping Newton's mathematical results?
options: Because 'force' was found to add nothing beyond the observed relation between acceleration and configuration
Because Einstein proved gravitation does not exist
Because Kepler's laws were shown to be false
Because quantum mechanics eliminated the concept of acceleration
quiz.explanation: Russell: to attribute planetary acceleration to the 'force' of gravitation 'was merely verbal, like saying that opium makes people sleep because it has a dormitive virtue'; equations could be written without invoking force at all.
quiz.related_concept: Newton's law of universal gravitation and the unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics

quiz.prompt: Match each figure to their key contribution: (1) Copernicus, (2) Kepler, (3) Galileo, (4) Newton -- to (A) law of universal gravitation, (B) heliocentric hypothesis, (C) three laws of planetary motion, (D) law of inertia and falling bodies.
quiz.explanation: Copernicus proposed heliocentrism, Kepler discovered the three laws of planetary motion, Galileo established inertia and the law of falling bodies, and Newton unified these into universal gravitation.
quiz.related_concept: Newton's law of universal gravitation and the unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics

essay_prompts.prompt: Evaluate Russell's response to E. A. Burtt's claim that the founders of modern science relied on unwarranted metaphysical assumptions and succeeded partly by luck. Is Russell's emphasis on method (tentative, evidence-based belief) an adequate defense?
rubric: Accurately states Burtt's challenge and Russell's response
Distinguishes between the content of early scientific theories and the method by which they were held
Engages with specific examples from the chapter (Copernicus, Kepler)

essay_prompts.prompt: Explain how the seventeenth-century removal of 'animism' and 'purpose' from physical explanation altered the relationship between science and theology, according to Russell, and why he considers this paradoxically to have both unsettled orthodoxy and revived human self-confidence.
rubric: Explains the shift from animistic to mechanistic explanation with reference to Aristotle's unmoved movers
Explains the diminishing role of continuous divine intervention
Explains the paradox of humbling cosmology producing human pride, with textual evidence
